items.q: The school choir (A) has performed at the town hall last Friday, and (B) everyone who attended (C) agreed it was (D) the best concert in years.
options: has performed at the town hall
items.explanation: A finished action with a past time expression (last Friday) takes the past simple, not the present perfect.

items.q: Each of the students (A) in our class (B) were asked to bring (C) a plant for the science fair (D) next week.
options: a plant for the science fair
items.explanation: Each of + plural noun is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular: was asked.

items.q: My uncle, who (A) works as a pilot, says that flying (B) over the Alps (C) at the night is far (D) more beautiful than most people imagine.
items.explanation: Times of day in fixed phrases take no article: at night, just like at noon and at midnight.

items.q: The documentary (A) explains how emperor penguins (B) survive the winter by huddling (C) close together while the females search (D) of food at sea.
items.explanation: The verb search takes the preposition for before the thing you are looking for.

items.q: Tourists were (A) amazing by the view from the tower, (B) which offers a (C) clear view of the whole valley (D) on sunny days.
options: clear view of the whole valley
items.explanation: The -ed participle describes how people feel: the tourists were amazed; amazing would describe the view itself.

items.q: My sister and (A) I bought a new tent, but (B) it's poles were broken, so (C) we returned it to the shop (D) the next morning.
options: we returned it to the shop
items.explanation: The possessive of it is its with no apostrophe; it's is short for it is.

items.q: The second half of the match was (A) much more exciting (B) than the first, and the crowd (C) got more louder (D) with every minute.
items.explanation: A one-syllable adjective forms its comparative with -er alone; more and -er are never used together.

items.q: We (A) could finish the poster for the fair today if (B) the printer (C) in the library (D) would work properly.
items.explanation: In a second conditional the if-clause takes the past simple; would belongs only in the main clause.

items.q: The coach (A) told to us that (B) the final had been moved (C) to Sunday because (D) of the storm warning.
items.explanation: Tell takes a direct object with no preposition (tell someone), unlike say to someone.

items.q: The girl (A) who sits beside me in maths, (B) which name I can never remember, (C) has just won (D) a national chess title.
options: who sits beside me in maths
which name I can never remember
items.correction: whose name I can never remember
items.explanation: To show possession inside a relative clause (her name) we use whose, not which.

items.q: My grandmother (A) still remembers (B) the day when (C) she saw first a television (D) in a neighbour's window.
items.explanation: An adverb like first goes before the main verb, never between the verb and its object.

items.q: Before the exam, the teacher (A) reminded us (B) to read every question (C) carefully and (D) do attention to the time.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is pay attention; the verb do does not combine with attention.

items.q: (A) Very few sunlight reaches the forest floor, (B) which is why the plants growing there (C) have developed (D) unusually large leaves.
items.explanation: Sunlight is uncountable, so it takes little; few is used only with plural countable nouns.

items.q: Tom wanted to join the cycling club, (A) but he (B) had neither a bike or a helmet, (C) so his cousin (D) lent him both.
options: had neither a bike or a helmet
items.correction: had neither a bike nor a helmet
items.explanation: The paired conjunction is neither … nor; neither is never followed by or.

items.q: By the time the fire engine (A) arrived, the neighbours (B) had already put out the flames, (C) so nobody has been hurt (D) that night.
options: had already put out the flames
items.explanation: The whole story is set in the finished past (that night), so the present perfect cannot be used; the past simple is needed.

items.q: Most of the equipment (A) in the chemistry lab (B) has been replaced, but (C) the microscopes (D) is still the same ones we used in grade six.
items.explanation: The subject the microscopes is plural, so the verb must be are; the singular has in the first clause agrees with equipment, not with microscopes.

items.q: (A) Sahara Desert is slowly expanding southwards, (B) and many scientists believe (C) that climate change (D) is partly to blame.
items.correction: The Sahara Desert is slowly expanding
items.explanation: Names of deserts, oceans, rivers and mountain ranges take the: the Sahara Desert.

items.q: Our neighbours (A) have lived (B) on the same house for twenty years, (C) so they know (D) every shopkeeper in the district.
items.explanation: We live in a house or a flat; on is used for streets and floors.

items.q: The chef (A) explained that (B) the secret of a good soup (C) is patient rather than (D) expensive ingredients.
options: the secret of a good soup
items.explanation: After the secret is a noun is needed to match ingredients; patience is the noun and patient the adjective.

items.q: The twins in my class look so (A) alike that even (B) their own teachers (C) sometimes confuse (D) they with each other.
items.explanation: The object of the verb confuse needs the object pronoun them, not the subject form they.

items.q: Mount Fansipan is (A) the higher mountain in Vietnam, (B) and thousands of hikers (C) attempt to reach (D) its summit every year.
items.explanation: Comparing one thing with all the others in a group (in Vietnam) needs the superlative the highest, not a comparative.

items.q: If people (A) recycled more glass, (B) factories will not need to use (C) so much raw sand, (D) which is running out in some regions.
options: factories will not need to use
which is running out in some regions
items.correction: factories would not need to use
items.explanation: A past-simple if-clause (second conditional) pairs with would in the main clause, not will.

items.q: The tour guide (A) warned us that the path (B) could be slippery and (C) asked if we brought (D) proper walking boots.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb (asked) the tense shifts back: "Have you brought…?" becomes had brought in reported speech.

items.q: The village (A) where my father grew up (B) has a small museum (C) full of tools (D) which farmers used them a century ago.
options: which farmers used them a century ago
items.correction: which farmers used a century ago
items.explanation: The relative pronoun which already acts as the object of used, so the extra pronoun them must be dropped.

items.q: (A) I wonder where did she buy that beautiful scarf, (B) because I (C) would like to get (D) one for my mother.
options: I wonder where did she buy
items.explanation: An indirect question keeps statement word order (subject before verb) and drops the auxiliary did.

items.q: Every morning my father (A) gets up at five, (B) does a short walk around the lake, (C) and then (D) reads the newspaper with his coffee.
options: does a short walk around the lake
reads the newspaper with his coffee
items.correction: takes a short walk around the lake
items.explanation: The natural collocation is take a walk or go for a walk; do a walk is not used in English.

items.q: There were (A) so many cars on the road (B) that we (C) wasted too many time (D) at every junction.
options: so many cars on the road
items.explanation: Time in this sense is uncountable, so it takes much; many is only for plural countable nouns.

items.q: My brother (A) practises the guitar (B) every evening (C) because he wants to join a band, (D) despite he has never played in public before.
options: because he wants to join a band
despite he has never played in public before
items.correction: although he has never played in public before
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and must be followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause needs the conjunction although.

items.q: (A) I am knowing the answer to this riddle, (B) but I'd rather let you (C) work it out (D) on your own.
items.explanation: Know is a stative verb, so it is not used in the continuous form; the present simple I know is needed.

items.q: Neither the coach (A) nor the players (B) was surprised when the referee (C) stopped the match (D) because of lightning.
items.explanation: With neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, and the players is plural, so were is needed.

items.q: The engineers (A) who designed (B) the tunnel under the sea had (C) to solve the hundreds of problems (D) nobody had faced before.
options: to solve the hundreds of problems
items.explanation: Used as a vague large quantity, hundreds of takes no article; the would only fit a specific, already-known set of problems.

items.q: The new app (A) lets you (B) translate street signs instantly, (C) which is (D) extreme useful for travellers who do not speak the local language.
items.explanation: An adverb (extremely) is needed to modify the adjective useful; extreme is itself an adjective.

items.q: (A) According with the latest weather report, (B) a strong typhoon will reach (C) the central coast (D) by Thursday evening.
options: According with the latest weather report
items.correction: According to the latest weather report
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is according to; with is never used after according.

items.q: This year's science fair (A) had (B) twice as many projects than last year's, (C) so the judges needed (D) an extra afternoon.
options: twice as many projects than last year's
items.correction: twice as many projects as last year's
items.explanation: Comparisons of equality use as … as; than belongs only with comparative forms such as more.

items.q: My parents (A) gave my sister and me a puppy (B) last month, and (C) her and me take turns (D) walking it before school.
options: gave my sister and me a puppy
items.explanation: The subject of take turns needs subject pronouns, she and I; the object forms her and me are correct only after a verb or preposition, as in segment A.

items.q: The film (A) had already started (B) when we (C) entered the cinema, so we (D) have missed the first ten minutes.
options: have missed the first ten minutes
items.explanation: The events belong to one finished past occasion, so the past simple missed is needed, not the present perfect.

items.q: Honey bees, (A) that are disappearing in many countries, (B) pollinate about a third (C) of the crops (D) we eat.
options: that are disappearing in many countries
items.correction: which are disappearing in many countries
items.explanation: A non-defining relative clause (between commas) must use which; that cannot follow a comma in this way.

items.q: Please (A) tell me (B) enough clearly what happened (C) at the bus stop (D) this morning so I can write it down.
options: this morning so I can write it down
items.explanation: Enough comes after the adverb or adjective it modifies (clearly enough); it goes before a noun only.

items.q: Our teacher (A) asked us to (B) work in pairs and (C) make a research on (D) the history of the local market.
options: the history of the local market
items.explanation: Research is uncountable and collocates with do: do research, not make a research.

items.q: The recipe (A) needs three eggs, (B) a cup of flour and (C) a pinch of salt, (D) but only few sugar.
items.explanation: Sugar is uncountable, so it takes a little; few goes only with plural countable nouns.
